narrative: The model estimates your chance of failing at 10%, so it sees a low but non-zero risk; under the school’s rule, that risk is treated as enough to require remedial courses. The strongest factor in the model’s reasoning was your record of past class failures: you have none, and that pushed the prediction toward passing rather than failing. The second strongest factor was your intention to pursue higher education; you want to continue studying, which also pushed toward passing. The third was your mother’s education level—5–9th grade—which modestly pushed toward passing in your case, though it is less common among students who passed than higher education. Because these top three signals are protective, the remedial requirement is best read as a cautious support decision: your profile has strengths, but other less influential information, especially your 10 school absences compared with an average of about four among passers and your very bad health status, likely keeps some concern alive. To improve, keep your no-failure record, protect your intention to continue to higher education, and reduce absences by addressing health and any barriers to attendance. Use family support and your internet access, keep study time steady, and ask for school support if attendance or health makes coursework harder. Remedial courses should be used as a structured way to close those gaps, not as a sign that your past performance is weak.
